findings.title: Durable pause and debt are written in one transaction with the most contended item, so routine concurrency loses both
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:115-128 (persistBillingPause, transact at :120); reserve ConditionCheck at spend.ts:75; app.ts:357-364 and :377/:385/:400; the false-green test is test/ledger.test.ts:115-127, which relies on the serial FakeTable at test/helpers.ts:189-210
findings.scenario: Instance A gets a maybe-billed or failed-settle outcome and calls persistBillingPause, which puts billing#pause and billingdebt#<event> in one TransactWriteItems. At the same moment instance B is reserving, and every reserve ConditionChecks billing#pause (and a second unresolved instance may also be putting billing#pause). DynamoDB's documented conflict rule cancels A's transaction with TransactionCanceledException [TransactionConflict]. Nothing retries it. The readback finds no pause, so pausePersisted=0 and neither the pause nor A's debt exists. B, and any fresh instance, keep calling the model after an unknown-usage event. The debt is lost too, even though its own item is never contended.
findings.evidence: Executed with a wrapper (backend-rt/ledger-faults/faultdb.ts) that adds DynamoDB conflict semantics: an in-flight transaction holds its items, and an overlapping transaction gets TransactionConflict. conflicts.test.ts C3 (API level): persistBillingPause returned false while B's reserve was in flight; B reserve ok; pause=false; debts=0. C3 (handler level): A returned E_MODEL_NO_USAGE with pausePersisted=false; B returned 200 with modelCalled=true; a fresh instance C returned 200 with modelCalled=true; 3 model calls in total. C4: two concurrent persists returned [true,false] and wrote only one debt (actual 15000). The package test 'persists each concurrent unresolved actual cost' expects [true,true], and passes only because FakeTable applies transactions one at a time. C2 (12 instances, 8 ms transactions), seed 1: settleFailed=2, debts=0, billing#pause absent, so two unresolved settlements left no durable trace at all. Seed 3: settleFailed=1, debts=0, no pause. The README and SPEC disclose that failed pause/debt storage stops only the current instance. They do not say the system's own reserve traffic causes this failure, or that the debt is lost along with the pause. The real-DynamoDB conflict behavior comes from AWS's documented transaction-conflict rules; it was not run against AWS.
findings.fix: Write billingdebt#<event> first as its own idempotent PutItem: it is uncontended, has no TTL, and needs no condition. Then put billing#pause in a separate call, either an unconditional overwrite or attribute_not_exists with ConditionalCheckFailed counted as success. Retry both a bounded number of times with jitter on TransactionConflict, throttling or a lost acknowledgment; that is safe because these are overwrites of fixed items, not money ADDs. Extend the test fake to model transaction conflicts and turn C3 and C4 into regression tests.

votes.reason: Reproduced with my own conflict-model wrapper (verify-ledger-faults-reproduce-it/txdb.ts plus f1f2.test.ts). The wrapper follows AWS's documented rule, which SPEC row 612 also cites: a TransactWriteItems that names an item held by an in-flight transaction is cancelled with TransactionConflict, and a ConditionCheck counts as naming the item. API level: persistBillingPause run while B's reserve held billing#pause returned false, left no pause and no debt, and B's reserve succeeded. Reversing the order cancels B's reserve (DdbError, so E_DDB) and the persist succeeds, so the outcome depends on arrival order. Two concurrent persists returned [true,false] and wrote only one debt (actual 15000). Handler level: A logged E_MODEL_NO_USAGE with pausePersisted=0; B returned 200; a fresh instance C returned 200; there were 3 model calls, no pause and no debts. In the natural F2 run, the E_SETTLE persist also conflicted with the same reserve that cancelled the settle, so that path often loses its pause too. The package test passes only because FakeTable.handle applies each transaction synchronously, so transactions never overlap. I downgrade from HIGH because the outcome is the disclosed path (README:62 and SPEC:288: instance-only stop, pausePersisted=0 logged and matched by the BillingAnomaly filter). Spend also stays bounded by per-request worst-case reservations and the caps, and every live model row is still blocked. The real defects are that the system's own reserve traffic causes the failure, inside a roughly 10-20 ms window, and that the uncontended debt is needlessly lost with it.

I confirmed the mechanism. I re-ran C3 and C4, which reproduced (persisted=false, pause=false, debts=0; C4 gave [true,false] with one debt). I also wrote my own test (mine.test.ts G1) that uses only the package FakeAws and returns a TransactionCanceledException with TransactionConflict or ThrottlingError on the persist transaction. persistBillingPause returned false, and neither billing#pause nor the uncontended billingdebt# item was written, because both share one TransactWriteItems (spend.ts:120). In the handler, A logged pausePersisted=0 and a fresh instance went on to call the model. The botocore DynamoDB model I fetched confirms the premise: an ongoing TransactWriteItems cancels a conflicting one, with CancellationReason TransactionConflict ('Transaction is ongoing for the item'). The package test at ledger.test.ts:115-127 passes only because FakeTable.apply commits each transaction synchronously and never models conflicts. Guards found elsewhere reduce the impact but do not prevent it. The instance is fenced in memory (pausedUntil=Infinity). The log line carries pausePersisted=0, which the BillingAnomaly filter matches, but the alarm has no actions. The full reservation stays on the month and day counters. The billing#<event> item stays 'reserved' for 100 days and the log line lasts 7 days, so 'no durable trace at all' (C2) is overstated. AWS Budgets' deny-Bedrock action is a delayed backstop. README item 15 and SPEC:288 already disclose that a failed pause write stops only the current instance. They do not disclose that the system's own reserve traffic causes the failure, or that the debt is lost along with the pause, which contradicts the 'persist every unresolved event' comment at spend.ts:112. A loss needs an anomaly plus an overlap of a few milliseconds with another reserve or persist (roughly 1-4% per anomaly at the 2 rps throttle). All three models are live-blocked at this commit, and spend stays bounded by the reservations. So this is MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

findings.title: A definite settle cancellation (TransactionConflict or throttle) causes a permanent service-wide pause and discards a valid paid answer
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:141-152 (settle catch); app.ts:400; table limit infra/aws/setup.yaml:423-425 (MaxWriteRequestUnits 50)
findings.scenario: Every reserve and every settle is a transaction on the same month and day counter items. When a settle overlaps another instance's reserve or settle, DynamoDB cancels it with TransactionConflict. That is a definite non-commit, but settle() handles it exactly like an ambiguous failure: it reads back state=reserved, returns false, and the app writes an E_SETTLE durable pause plus debt. The service then stays stopped until the owner reconciles. The visitor's paid, checked answer is thrown away, and the counters keep the full reservation. Overlapping reserves fail the same way and return E_DDB 503s.
findings.evidence: conflicts.test.ts C1: a TransactionConflict cancellation on the settle transaction gave 503 E_SETTLE, pausePersisted=true and one debt, with counters at 9205 against actual 2596. A fresh instance then got E_BILLING_PAUSE. C2: 8 of 12 requests got E_DDB from reserve conflicts. sim.test.ts S1 (Poisson arrivals at the 2 rps API Gateway default, 20 ms transactions, time scaled 1:20): the first durable E_SETTLE pause came at request #1, #5, #7 and #5 across four seeds. This overestimates real frequency because of timer granularity. An analytic estimate, 1-exp(-4/s x 2 x 10-20 ms), gives about 8-15% of settles conflicting at sustained 2 rps. Real frequency is suspected; the code path was executed.
findings.fix: On a DdbError whose CancellationReasons show a definite non-commit (TransactionConflict, ThrottlingError or ProvisionedThroughputExceeded) and a consistent readback showing state=reserved, retry the settle a bounded number of times with backoff and a fresh ClientRequestToken. The event-state CAS keeps the retry idempotent, so it is not a blind ADD. Pause only after the retries are exhausted or the failure is truly ambiguous. Apply the same bounded retry to a definitely cancelled reserve, which is safe because nothing committed and a new event id is used.

votes.reason: Reproduced in f1f2.test.ts F2. A's model returned a valid reply while B's reserve held spend#month. A's settle was cancelled with TransactionConflict, the readback showed state=reserved, settle() returned false, and app.ts:400 called pause('E_SETTLE'). A got 503 with the answer discarded. A's event stayed 'reserved' (9205) against an actual of 2596, so the counters over-count. When the persist did not also conflict, billing#pause reason=E_SETTLE and one debt were written, and fresh instance C got 503 E_BILLING_PAUSE, a service-wide stop until the owner reconciles. When it did conflict (the natural timing), pausePersisted=0 and no durable stop was written. Nothing in settle() tells a definite TransactionConflict non-commit apart from an ambiguous outcome. SPEC:282 discloses reserve conflicts as an availability trade-off, but not settle conflicts turning into a durable pause. Real frequency is lower than at a sustained 2 rps, because per-connection limits (10 per 10 min) and the roughly $2.50/day budget cap the requests that reach a reservation. Still, a short burst from a few distinct connections or /64s can trigger it at little cost, and the resulting stop lasts until the owner acts.

Reproduced independently (mine.test.ts G2): a TransactionCanceledException with TransactionConflict, or with ThrottlingError, on the settle transaction gave 503 E_SETTLE and pausePersisted=true. The month counter stayed at 9205 against an actual cost of 2596, and a fresh instance got E_BILLING_PAUSE. G3 shows the same thing for release() after a not-billed model error. The settle catch at spend.ts:145-151 never inspects cancellationReasons. A consistent readback showing 'reserved' after a definite cancellation is therefore treated like an ambiguous failure, and app.ts:377 and :400 write an owner-only durable pause. I found no guard that prevents this. There is no retry, and nothing clears the pause automatically. SPEC:282 accepts conflicts only as an availability cost for reserve, not as a cause of a durable, owner-reconciled outage after settle. Every reserve and every settle touches the same month and day items, so the per-request risk scales with concurrent transaction rate times hold time: rare at low traffic, a few percent per request at the 2 rps throttle. The OnDemand MaxWriteRequestUnits of 50 adds a throttling route under bursts. The S1 simulation overestimates frequency because of timer granularity, as the finding itself says. The direction is safe for money (it over-counts), so MEDIUM.

findings.title: Nothing checks the 28 s Lambda deadline; a kill after the model call leaves no debt, no durable pause and no log line
findings.location: packages/explain/src/app.ts:367 (callModel without a remaining-time check); bedrock.ts:9 (MODEL_TIMEOUT_MS 20000); dynamodb.ts:23 (3000); infra/aws/explain.yaml:208 (Timeout: 28); index.ts:20 (handler ignores context); event TTL at spend.ts:78; alarm filter at explain.yaml:164
findings.scenario: Before the model call the handler can make up to about 8 sequential AWS round trips: settings, pause read, headroom read, salt put, salt deletes, two rate counters, and the reserve. Each may take up to 3 s, and then the model call may take 20 s. With DynamoDB at about 1 s per call and the model at 19.5-20 s, the settle or pause transaction starts after 28 s, and Lambda kills the instance. What remains is a 'reserved' event with a 100-day TTL. There is no billingdebt record, no billing#pause and no application log line, so the BillingAnomaly metric filter cannot fire. Fresh instances keep calling. The worst case for the model timeout path (maybe-billed, which explicitly requires a fleet-wide stop) is the one most likely to cross the deadline. The reservation still covers the verified worst case, so there is no unreserved call, but the claims 'unknown usage ... stop further spend, including fresh instances' and 'every ambiguous settlement keeps ... a no-TTL debt' do not hold here.
findings.evidence: deadline.test.ts D1, a warmed engine with latencies scaled 1:100 measured on the real handler path. With every call just under its timeout, the model ended at about 44.0 s and the settle at about 46.9 s. With DynamoDB at about 1 s and a valid but slow model, the model ended at 28.0 s and the settle started at 28.06 s. With DynamoDB at about 1 s and the model timing out (usage unknown), the model ended at 28.5 s and the pause transaction started at 28.5 s. With DynamoDB at about 1.4 s and a 20 s model, the pause started at 31.7 s. D2 left the model call or the settle transaction hanging to stand in for the kill: pause=false, debts=0, reservedEvents=1, eventTtlDays=100, logLines=0; a fresh instance returned 200 with modelCalled=true.
findings.fix: Pass the Lambda context's remaining time into the handler. Before callModel, require remaining time of at least the model timeout plus the settle, readback and persist budget plus a margin; otherwise release the reservation and answer busy. Alternatively, derive every per-call timeout from one invocation deadline. Remove the TTL from 'reserved' events, or set it only at settlement, so stale unresolved events stay as evidence. Add an alarm on AWS/Lambda Errors or timeouts next to BillingAnomaly.

votes.reason: Timeline reproduced in f3.test.ts with latencies scaled 1:100. A cold instance on the day's first request makes 8 sequential round trips before the model: the settings reads (run in parallel), the pause read, the headroom reads, the salt put, the salt deletes, two countUps and the reserve. With DynamoDB and settings at 1 s and a 19.5 s model, the settle started at 28.2 s. With a 20 s model timeout, the pause transaction started at 28.47 s. Warm instance at 1 s: 25.3 s. The kill stand-in (a transaction after the model hangs) left logLines=0, pause=false and debts=0, with the event 'reserved' under a 100-day TTL, and a fresh instance returned 200. index.ts ignores the Lambda context, and no remaining-time check exists. I grade it LOW because the kill needs about 1 s for every DynamoDB call, or several 3 s DynamoDB timeouts right after a near-20 s model call. Under normal latencies (20 ms DynamoDB, 200 ms settings) the settle started at 21.2 s, leaving about 6.8 s of margin. In those degraded conditions the persist would probably fail anyway; what is newly lost is the log line, and with it the alarm metric, plus the in-memory instance pause.

Confirmed by inspection and by re-running D1 and D2. index.ts exports createHandler(...), whose function takes only the event and ignores the Lambda context. No src file reads the remaining time. Per-call timeouts are DDB 3 s, settings 3 s and model 20 s, against a Lambda Timeout of 28. D2 reproduced the result of a kill: pause=false, debts=0, one reserved event with a 100-day TTL, no log line, and a fresh instance that calls the model. The only alarm in the templates is BillingAnomaly, and it has no actions; nothing alarms on AWS/Lambda Errors. Guards elsewhere limit the impact: the reservation stays counted (safe over-count), the reserved event stays as evidence for 100 days, and the Budget action is a backstop. The scenario also needs about 7-8 s of slow but successful pre-model AWS calls (any call that hits its 3 s timeout fails closed before the model) together with a model call near the full 20 s. That is a rare correlated brownout. The gap is real but unlikely, so LOW.

findings.title: A lost or late reserve acknowledgment leaks the reservation permanently with no debt; leaks can exhaust the daily cap with zero model calls
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:81-93 (reserve catch and readback); spend.ts:78 (event TTL 100 days)
findings.scenario: The reserve transaction commits, but the reply is lost and the consistent readback also fails, or the commit lands after the readback. The request fails closed with E_DDB and no model call, but the reserved micros stay on the month and day counters indefinitely. No debt is written, and the leaked event looks identical to a D2 killed-mid-call event: both are 'reserved' with no debt. A DynamoDB brownout therefore uses up the day's budget without spending anything and stops the service until the next day.
findings.evidence: misc.test.ts M1: 27 consecutive E_DDB results, then E_HEADROOM; modelCalls=0; the day counter reached 248535 of the 250000 test cap; 27 reserved events, 0 debts, no pause. M2 (late commit): E_DDB with modelCalled=false, then the month counter was 9205 with one reserved event and 0 debts.
findings.fix: Accept as fail-closed but document it. Owner reconciliation needs a way to tell 'reserved, model never called' from 'reserved, call outcome unknown'. For example, set a calledAt attribute on the event with a CAS before callModel (one extra write), or retry the readback once after a short delay.

votes.reason: Reproduced in f4to7.test.ts F4 with the reserve acknowledgment lost and the event readback failing. The run gave 27 consecutive E_DDB results, then E_HEADROOM, with 0 model calls. The day counter reached 248535 of a 250000 cap, with 27 'reserved' events, 0 debts and no pause. This is the intended fail-closed design (the code comment and SPEC:282 say only a proven reservation permits a call, and nothing refunds an unproven one). No money is spent, but reconciliation cannot tell these events apart from a killed-mid-call event.

Re-ran M1 and M2, and both reproduced: 27 E_DDB then E_HEADROOM, modelCalls=0, day counter 248535/250000, 27 reserved events, 0 debts; M2 gave month 9205, one reserved event, 0 debts. In the code, the reserve catch at spend.ts:81-93 returns ok only on a proven readback and otherwise throws E_DDB. No path releases, records or flags a reservation that may have committed. This is fail-closed: no model call is ever made without a proven reservation. The cost is availability and lost monthly allowance, and SPEC:282 does not say leaked reservations stay counted. The day counter resets daily, but the month counter does not, so the leak is real and not prevented elsewhere. Impact is limited to availability, so LOW.

findings.title: Debt records can describe settlements that actually committed; following the README during reconciliation would undercount
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:145-151 (settle readback); app.ts:400; README.md:62 ('Each ambiguous settlement retains its reservation')
findings.scenario: A settle commits after its readback (late commit), or it commits with the bound pause but the pause readback fails. The app then writes an E_SETTLE debt plus pause even though the event is settled and the counters already hold the actual cost, not the reservation. An owner who trusts the README and adjusts counters by (actual - reserved) for each debt would subtract twice. In the M7 case the pause reason E_PROVIDER_BOUND is also overwritten with E_SETTLE.
findings.evidence: misc.test.ts M3: counters 2596/2596, event state settled with actual 2596, yet the debt says reserved 9205, actual 2596, reason E_SETTLE. M7: counters 112640 equal actual, and the log/eval code and the debt reason were E_SETTLE rather than E_PROVIDER_BOUND.
findings.fix: Reconciliation must read billing#<event>.state and settle only events still 'reserved'. Record in the debt that the settlement state was unknown. Change the README wording from 'retains its reservation' to 'reservation or settled amount, check the event state'.

votes.reason: Reproduced in F5. First case: the settle committed, its acknowledgment was lost and the readback failed. Second case: the settle committed 30 ms after the readback. In both, the event was 'settled' with actual 2596 and both counters were 2596, yet the code was E_SETTLE and the debt read reserved 9205, actual 2596, reason E_SETTLE. README:62's 'Each ambiguous settlement retains its reservation' is wrong for these cases. M7 also reproduced: a bound-violation settle committed with its pause, the pause readback failed, and the pause and debt reasons were overwritten to E_SETTLE. The log still carries billedBoundViolated=1, so that fact is not fully lost. No reconciliation procedure is documented, so the undercount harm depends on how the owner reconciles. The doc inaccuracy is real.

Re-ran M3 and M7, and both reproduced. In M3 the event is 'settled' with actual 2596 and the counters are 2596, yet the debt says reserved 9205, actual 2596, reason E_SETTLE. In M7 the E_PROVIDER_BOUND pause reason is overwritten with E_SETTLE. The code allows this: the settle readback can run before a late commit, or the pause readback can fail after the commit. The guard elsewhere is partial. The debt carries the event key, and SPEC:285 says event state is stored in the table. No documented procedure tells the owner to adjust counters by actual minus reserved for each debt, so the double subtraction is hypothetical. Still, README:62 says each ambiguous settlement 'retains its reservation', which is wrong in these cases. A documentation-precision issue, so LOW.

findings.title: reserve() readback runs even after a definite cancellation and is unguarded, so a pause refusal can surface as E_DDB
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:84
findings.scenario: The reserve transaction is cancelled by the billing#pause ConditionCheck, a definite refusal, and then the readback GetItem throws. The error propagates as E_DDB, so the instance is not fenced (pausedUntil stays 0) and the log shows the wrong cause. The next request's pre-read catches the pause, so the effect is small.
findings.evidence: misc.test.ts M7b: code E_DDB, pausedUntil 0, modelCalls 0.
findings.fix: Map the CancellationReasons first when the error is a TransactionCanceledException with ConditionalCheckFailed. Do the readback only for ambiguous failures, inside try/catch.

votes.reason: Confirmed. At API level, with billing#pause present and the event readback failing, reserve threw DdbError instead of returning which:'pause'. At handler level, a pause written between the pre-read and the reserve plus a failed readback gave E_DDB, pausedUntil 0 and 0 model calls, and the next request got E_BILLING_PAUSE from the pre-read. Two coincident conditions are needed, and the only effects are a wrong log code and one unfenced instance until its next pre-read.

Confirmed. At spend.ts:84 the GetItem runs before cancellationReasons are inspected and sits outside any try/catch. If it throws, the DdbError propagates to app.ts:350 as E_DDB, and pausedUntil stays 0. M7b reproduced this (E_DDB, pausedUntil 0, modelCalls 0). The impact is negligible. No model call is made, the visitor still gets 503 paused, and the next request's billingPaused pre-read at app.ts:312 fences the instance. Only the log code and the in-memory fence differ. LOW, close to informational.

findings.title: Cache-write tokens are charged at the base input price, which undercounts if they ever occur (suspected)
findings.location: packages/explain/src/aws/bedrock.ts:56-62 (usageOf) and comment at :49
findings.scenario: inTok = inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens, all priced at the input rate. The comment says cached input is 'conservatively' charged at the uncached price. That is true for cache reads (about 0.1x) but not for cache writes, which Anthropic prices at about 1.25x base input for 5-minute writes and 2x for 1-hour writes (Bedrock sets its own prices). A nonzero cacheWrite would make actualMicros low and could hide an overrun from the actual > reserved check. No cachePoint is sent, so this should normally be zero.
findings.evidence: Code inspection only; not executed. Multipliers come from the bundled claude-api reference (cache_creation about 1.25x, cache_read about 0.1x).
findings.fix: Treat cacheWriteInputTokens > 0 as unexplained usage and return maybe-billed, or price it with a reviewed per-model write multiplier. Fix the comment.

votes.reason: The code fact is confirmed: usage with cacheWriteInputTokens 300 gave inTok 310, all priced at the input rate, so the 'conservatively' comment is imprecise for cache writes. The scenario cannot arise with the reviewed request, though. The captured body has only system, messages, inferenceConfig and additionalModelRequestFields, with no cachePoint, and on Bedrock prompt-cache writes require an explicit cachePoint. If writes did occur, inTok still includes them and is checked against inputBoundTokens (prompt bytes plus framing). Prompt bytes far exceed token counts for text, so a 1.25x or 2x write premium could not realistically hide an overrun of the reservation. I could not confirm any path that triggers it. A comment fix or fail-closed handling would be a nit.

Guards elsewhere prevent this. The request shape is closed and never carries a cachePoint: modelRequest builds only system, messages, inferenceConfig and the reviewed requestFields, and converse.test.ts:21 rejects any request matching /cachePoint/. SPEC:89 says prompt caching is deliberately not used. On Bedrock, cache writes need an explicit cachePoint, so cacheWriteInputTokens should always be 0. Separately, the overrun check at app.ts:394 compares token counts (inTok, which includes write tokens, against inputBoundTokens = prompt bytes + framing), so the price multiplier cannot hide a token-bound breach. And because the reservation prices input bytes rather than tokens, a 1.25x write premium on realistic token counts stays well under it. What remains is an imprecise comment at bedrock.ts:49 and infra/aws/README.md:177, which say write tokens are charged 'conservatively'. That is a documentation nit, not a reachable undercount. Not executed by the finder.

findings.title: Table replacement or deletion silently erases the durable pause, debts and month counter; the setup comment is stale
findings.location: infra/aws/setup.yaml:411-419 (comment 'Every item has a TTL'; DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy Delete)
findings.scenario: Pause and debt items deliberately have no TTL, so 'Every item has a TTL' is wrong. A setup-stack update that replaces the table (for example a TableName or key-schema change), or deleting the stack, removes billing#pause, every billingdebt# and spend#<month>. That re-opens the full monthly allowance and clears a durable stop with no owner reconciliation. SPEC:524 covers deletion but not replacement on update.
findings.evidence: Inspection of setup.yaml lines 411-438; not executed (no AWS).
findings.fix: Set UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy to Retain, or set DeletionProtectionEnabled: true, for the counter table. Correct the comment. Add a test_templates.py assertion.

votes.reason: The stale comment is confirmed: setup.yaml says 'Every item has a TTL', but billing#pause and billingdebt# have none (SPEC:53, :333). DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy are both Delete, and DeletionProtectionEnabled is false, which test_templates.py:460-463 deliberately pins. The risk is narrower than stated. Deletion is disclosed with a reconcile-first instruction at SPEC:524. The table has the fixed custom name 'biasclear-explain', hardcoded as EXPLAIN_TABLE at explain.yaml:219, so CloudFormation refuses a same-name replacement such as a key-schema change. Only a deliberate rename would replace the table and silently drop the pause and debts. Retain or deletion protection, plus fixing the comment, remains a reasonable hardening.

The 'silent replacement' scenario is guarded. TableName is pinned to 'biasclear-explain' (setup.yaml:421, asserted in test_templates.py:455), and CloudFormation refuses any update that would replace a custom-named resource unless the name also changes. A rename would also have to change EXPLAIN_TABLE in explain.yaml:219, which is a deliberate, reviewed act on the owner's setup stack, not a silent update. Stack deletion is an explicit owner action, and SPEC:524 already requires reconciling unresolved charges and preserving billing evidence before it. DeletionPolicy Delete and DeletionProtectionEnabled false are a deliberate privacy choice, asserted by tests. The only real residue is the stale 'Every item has a TTL' comment at setup.yaml:412 (pause and debt items have no TTL) and the matching test name; that is a documentation nit.

findings.title: Any settlement or release that loses a normal DynamoDB transaction conflict is treated as uncertain and turns into a permanent no-TTL billing pause
findings.location: packages/explain/src/spend.ts:141-152 (settle catch returns false on any error); packages/explain/src/app.ts:377 and :400 (false leads to pause('E_SETTLE')); infra/aws/setup.yaml:425 (MaxWriteRequestUnits 50)
findings.scenario: Request A has a normal answer (actual 2,596 micros, reserved 9,205). It settles while request B's reservation transaction is still in progress on the same hot keys (spend#month and spendday#day). DynamoDB cancels A's settle with CancellationReasons TransactionConflict, which means nothing was written. settle() reads the event back, finds it still 'reserved', and returns false. The app then writes billing#pause with reason E_SETTLE and no TTL. Every instance stays paused until the owner reconciles by hand, even though no money anomaly happened. A model that answers 429 (never billed) and then has its release collide the same way also creates a permanent pause. One client can trigger this inside the per-IP limit (10 per 10 min) by sending a burst of about 5 concurrent requests, because their settles and reservations overlap on the two shared counter items.
findings.evidence: Executed with backend-rt/ledger-logic/conflict.test.ts and lock.ts. lock.ts layers DynamoDB's documented transaction-conflict behaviour (the same behaviour SPEC.md:612 cites) on top of FakeAws, which itself never conflicts. Output: A got 503 with code E_SETTLE, actualMicros 2596 < reservedMicros 9205, no overrun or bound flag, and pausePersisted 1. The recorded conflict was on locked keys spend#2026-10 and spendday#2026-10-05. The billing#pause item has no ttl. A fresh instance at 2026-11-14 (40 days later, next month) got 503 E_BILLING_PAUSE and made no model call. Second test: 429 model plus a release conflict gave E_SETTLE with actualMicros 0 and a persisted pause. SPEC.md:282 acknowledges conflicts only for reservations, not settlement. Also suspected, not executed: the table's on-demand write maximum (50 WCU/s) against roughly 14-16 WCU per request (transactional items cost 2 WCU each) means a 5-request burst can get a settle throttled, which leads to the same permanent pause.
findings.fix: In settle() and persistBillingPause(), look at cancellationReasons. If DynamoDB definitively cancelled the transaction (TransactionCanceledException with no ConditionalCheckFailed on the event, for example TransactionConflict or ThrottlingError), retry the identical transaction a few times with jitter, using the same ClientRequestToken. That retry is safe: the event CAS `#s = :reserved` and the token mean an ADD can never apply twice. Only an outcome that is still ambiguous after the retries (transport timeout or network error with no proof from the read-back) should take the durable-pause path. B's model then returns 403 AccessDenied (not billed, pauseInstance), which sets pausedUntil = B.start + 15m = T+30m-10s. Request C in [T+30m-10s, T+30m+5s) passes step 1, skips step 2 because now < nextSettingsCheck, and calls Bedrock with logging ON. (2) Midnight window: B starts at 23:59:59 on a cached pass and waits on DynamoDB. A's check at 00:00 fails (logging ON) and pauses until 00:15. B then hits E_HEADROOM and sets pausedUntil = nextDayStart(23:59:59) = 00:00. From 00:00 to 00:15 every request skips the privacy read and reaches Bedrock. This is latent at this head: all three models are blocked, and a standard Lambda (explain.yaml sets no capacity provider) runs one invocation per environment. It still breaks the SPEC §4 promise that a changed setting pauses Explain, under exactly the concurrency the design says it handles. findings.fix: Never let a failed verdict act as a cache hit. On failure set nextSettingsCheck = 0 (or keep a separate settingsOkUntil that only a pass sets), so the first request after any pause rechecks. Make every pausedUntil write monotonic: state.pausedUntil = Math.max(state.pausedUntil, x). Optionally clear settingsCheck only if it is still the promise this request awaited. findings.title: ops.sh does not enforce model readiness itself; only the workflow step does
findings.location: infra/aws/ops.sh:276 (deploy), ops.sh:308 (evaluate), ops.sh:346 (switch on) all call model-table.mjs --check-key, which exits 0 for any key in the table (model-table.mjs:182-187). The real gate is readiness.mjs, which only .github/workflows/explain.yml:206-212 runs.

findings.evidence: `node infra/aws/model-table.mjs --check-key sonnet55` exits 0, while `node infra/aws/readiness.mjs --model sonnet55` exits 1. I imported the built dist/index.mjs (the zip's only file) with an otherwise valid env for each of the three models (backend-rt/privacy-gate/bundle-probe.mjs). 'An operator runs ops.sh with credentials outside the workflow' cannot happen. signin() (ops.sh:43-68) ignores ambient keys. findings.title: Privacy-read parsers are lenient: a missing or miscased loggingConfig, or any unrelated 200 JSON object, reads as 'logging off'; runtime and ops.sh disagree on arrays; retention reads only .mode
findings.location: packages/explain/src/aws/bedrock.ts:240-241 (loggingOn), bedrock.ts:243-246 (mode only), infra/aws/ops.sh:193 (jq), ops.sh:212
findings.scenario: If a 200 response arrives in an unexpected shape, such as {"LoggingConfig":{…}}, {"message":"Rate exceeded"}, or a duplicate key whose last value is null, both the runtime and ops.sh conclude that logging is off. The runtime treats {"loggingConfig":[]} as off, while ops.sh treats it as on. Retention ignores every field except mode, so per-model or pending overrides, if the API has them, would go unseen. That last point is suspected: the API shape cannot be checked offline. Real AWS is unlikely to send these, but the parse fails open on any unknown shape.
findings.evidence: backend-rt/privacy-gate/logging-parse.test.ts prints a table. {}, {"loggingConfig":null}, {"loggingConfig":{}}, {"LoggingConfig":{s3Config}} and {"message":"Rate exceeded"} read as runtime=off and ops.sh=off. {"loggingConfig":[]} reads as runtime=off and ops.sh=on. Empty CLI stdout reads as ops.sh='' and is treated as off. That last case matches the AWS CLI printing nothing for an empty {} response, which test_ops_settings_rt.py confirms.
findings.fix: Treat logging as off only when the body's key set is a subset of {loggingConfig} and loggingConfig is null or {}. Treat any other key, an array, or a non-object as unreadable (pause). Require an exact key set for retention responses too, and update the jq to match.

votes.reason: I reproduced the parse table (verify-privacy-gate-reproduce-it/parse.test.ts). {}, {loggingConfig:null}, {loggingConfig:{}}, {LoggingConfig:{...}} and {message:'Rate exceeded'} read as off in both the runtime and ops.sh. {loggingConfig:[]} reads as off in the runtime and on in ops.sh. No reachable input produces these shapes, though. getJson (bedrock.ts:226-228) throws on any non-200, which covers throttling and auth errors, and on any non-object body, and readAccountSettings (bedrock.ts:244-245) throws on a non-string retention mode. Both read paths are SigV4-signed TLS requests to bedrock.<region>.amazonaws.com, whose REST-JSON member is `loggingConfig`. A non-empty config, even {textDataDeliveryEnabled:false}, reads as on. The array disagreement has no producible input. The retention-overrides point is speculative and cannot be checked offline. An exact-key-set parser would also start pausing whenever AWS adds a response field. This is hardening only.

The shapes that break the parser cannot come from the API. The Bedrock service model (botocore 1.43.103, bedrock/2023-04-20) defines GetModelInvocationLoggingConfigurationResponse with a single member, loggingConfig, whose members are cloudWatchConfig, s3Config and the *DataDeliveryEnabled flags. GetAccountDataRetentionResponse has only mode (required) and updatedAt, so the suspected per-model or pending retention overrides do not exist. getJson (bedrock.ts:215-230) accepts only HTTP 200 with a JSON object, over SigV4/TLS to bedrock.<region>.amazonaws.com. 'Rate exceeded' comes as 429/400, which throws and gives E_SETTINGS_READ. The cases read as off ({}, null, {}) are the API's real off states. A capitalized key, an array or duplicate keys cannot come from the REST-JSON contract. On the array case the runtime and ops.sh do disagree, and ops.sh is the stricter of the two. An exact-key-set check would only be hardening.

Durable pause fences reservations atomically: the reserve transaction's ConditionCheck on billing#pause refuses a pause written between the pre-read and the transaction (package test). A committed pause plus fresh instance gives E_BILLING_PAUSE.
Durable pause survives instance and month changes: M5 wrote it at Oct 31 23:59:59.9, and a fresh instance on 2027-11-30 got E_BILLING_PAUSE. Pause and debt items have no ttl attribute.

Conditional settlement and no double-settle: M4 ran four concurrent settle/settle/release/settle(9000) calls on one reservation, giving [true,true,false,false] with the month and day counters at exactly 3000. M4b, with conflict semantics, also ended at 3000. The CAS on state=reserved is the fence.

Consistent recovery after a lost acknowledgment: a lost reserve acknowledgment with a successful consistent readback permits exactly one model call (package test). A lost settle acknowledgment is proven by event state plus actual, with no second ADD (package test counts 3 TransactWriteItems and 0 UpdateItem).

No blind ADD retries: transport.ts and Ddb.call never retry; settle failure never re-sends a counter ADD; M1 shows one reserve transaction per request; ops.sh invokes with AWS_MAX_ATTEMPTS=1, one invoke at a time.

Duplicate or stale event ids: event ids are server-side randomUUID values, the event Put is conditioned on attribute_not_exists(pk), no client field reaches the ledger keys, and the settle ClientRequestToken always differs from the reserve token.
Month and day rollover: keys are fixed at request start, and settle uses the reservation's keys. M5 touched only spend#2026-10 and spendday#2026-10-31; the package test covers settle after midnight.
Bound breach settles the real charge and persists the stop atomically with the settlement (package test; M7 counters 112640 equal actual), and the answer is discarded with 503 paused.
Unknown usage keeps the full reservation and is not reported as an actual cost: in the D1 maybe-billed case and the package tests, actualMicros stays unset.

Clock skew is bounded, with a caveat: keys come from the local clock, so an instance 5 s fast booked into November while October was full (M6). Exposure is limited to reservations made inside the skew window; Lambda uses Amazon Time Sync. Informational, not a finding.
Settle, release and persistBillingPause never throw into the handler (all failures become false), so a ledger failure cannot surface as an unlogged E_INTERNAL after a model call.
